Slide 1 (title):
Staying Organized: Managing your Email

   ●​ Ask students what they know about email/ keeping their email organized to
      activate prior knowledge

Slide 2:

Why is keeping your email organized important?

***allow students to answer verbally before explaining:

   ●​ So you don't miss any important emails (missing classwork, schedule change for work or

       for a test, additional information about an assignment or event)

   ●​ People use email to communicate important information about events that may occur

       before or after school

   ●​ People also use email to communicate when you may be missing work or you need to

       see them during RAMs time

   ●​ If you apply to a job they may email you information about what you need to bring, when

       you need to be there, your schedule, etc.

   ●​ People may try to schedule meetings or interviews with you

What could happen if you miss an important email?

***allow students to answer verbally before explaining

   ●​ You could miss an important date or assignment

           ○​ For work you could miss an interview or a schedule change

           ○​ For school you could miss an important meeting date or your teacher requesting

              to meet with you about an assignment or test

Slide 3:

How can you keep your email organized?

***allow students to answer verbally before explaining

   ●​ Delete emails that you do not need, we will talk more about this in a minute
    ●​ Star important emails

   ●​ Create folders to organize emails if you think it is necessary

   ●​ Write down any actions you need to take

Slide 4:

When should you delete or reply to emails?

***allow students to answer verbally before explaining on the next slides

Slide 5:

When should you delete an email

  ●​   Delete emails after you have completed the task

  ●​   If the email is old and you do not need it anymore

  ●​   Spam emails

  ●​   Unimportant emails (coupons, advertisements)

Slide 6:

When should you reply to an email?

  ●​   If someone is asking you a question

  ●​   To let someone know you have seen their email

  ●​   If there is a task that needs to be completed (you don't always need to reply to these)

  ●​   If you have any follow-up questions to an email

Slide 7:

When should you take action?

   ●​ When you need to complete something/turn something in

   ●​ When you need to add something to your calender

   ●​ When you need to get something signed

   ●​ When you need to bring something in
 Slides 8-11: Lets try

Read the example and allow students to decide and answer verbally whether they would reply

to, delete, or take action on an email

Slide 8: reply because someone is asking you to confirm something

Slide 9: delete because this email is most likely fake (no subject, weird link, no sender at the

end of the email)

Slide 10: delete, your teacher doesn't need anything from you, they are just letting you know

they got your assignment. You may want to save the email and delta it after your grade has

been entered.

Slide 11: take action, this email does not necessarily need a reply, it just needs an action to be

taken

essential_questions: ●​ How can I keep track of the money I earn?
●​ How do I make a deposit and what does it mean to save money in a bank account?
●​ How can I tell whether I have enough money to buy something I want?
●​ Why is it important to be responsible with money?
materials: ●​ Earned cash (one-dollar bills and/or coins collected throughout the week)
●​ Bankability computer program (student laptops + teacher computer)
objectives: By the end of the lesson, students will:
●​ Count earned cash (one-dollar bills and/or coins) with increasing independence or with appropriate adult
support.
●​ Complete or participate in completing a deposit slip by recording the correct dollar amount.
●​ Navigate the Bankability program to locate their account balance, deposit earnings, and view any bills
due.
●​ Demonstrate understanding that money can be deposited, saved, or used to purchase items from the
school store.
●​ Communicate during the banking routine using their established method (AAC device, speech, pointing,
gestures, or writing).
●​ Demonstrate targeted skills with at least 80% accuracy with IEP accommodations and prompting as
needed.
prior_knowledge: How will you activate prior knowledge, build background, or review previous lessons?
●​ Students have participated in Bankability throughout the school year and are familiar with earning and
depositing money.
●​ They have practiced counting dollar bills in previous Life Skills Math lessons.
●​ Prior lessons have introduced vocabulary: "deposit," "bank account," "balance," and "bills."
●​ Activation for Group 1: Using the AAC device and visuals, ask "What do we do on Bankability day?"
during the greeting routine.
●​ Activation for Group 2: Brief verbal exchange during entry — "What do we do on Bankability day?"
and "What does it mean to deposit money?"
sequence: Learning activities/strategies, student application, monitoring of performance:
── GROUP 1 (approx. 0–45 min) ──
0–5 min | Entry & Setup
Students enter and are assisted by TA/PCAs in locating their math folder and a deposit slip. Student teacher uses
the AAC device to individually model "hello" to each student, accepting any communicative response. Visual
schedule is reviewed.
5–10 min | Count Money & Fill Out Deposit Slip
Each student (with adult support as needed) counts earned cash using least-to-most prompting. Students write or
have an adult scribe the total on their deposit slip. AAC device models functional vocabulary: "count," "money,"
"deposit," "how much."
10–40 min | Individual Banking Rotation
Student teacher calls students to the bank (teacher desk/computer) one at a time. At the bank:
Student teacher and student count the money together to verify the total.
Student teacher enters the deposit into Bankability and adds the weekly $100 paycheck.
Student teacher tells the student their new balance and whether any bills are due.
If the student has enough money after bills, they may shop at the school store, communicating their choice
via AAC, pointing, or gesture.
While waiting, students are supported by TA/PCAs with deposit slips, quiet tasks, or regulation supports. Cool
Math Games is available as a structured wait activity.
40–45 min | Closure & Transition (Group 1)
Student teacher briefly reviews: "Today we made a deposit and checked our balance." Each student is prompted
to indicate one banking action (via AAC, gesture, or verbal). Students earn reward cash for participation. Group 1
transitions out.
── TRANSITION (approx. 45–55 min) ──
Group 2 enters and locates their math folder and a deposit slip. Students begin a 10-minute snack and leisure
break. Timer is posted. Student teacher and TA reset the banking station.
── GROUP 2 (approx. 55–90 min) ──
55–65 min | Independent Money Counting & Deposit Slip Completion
After the break timer ends, students sit at workstations. Student teacher briefly reviews: "What are we doing
today?" Students independently count earned cash and complete their deposit slip (name, date, amount). Student
teacher circulates to check accuracy.
65–85 min | Individual Banking Rotation
Student teacher calls students to the bank one at a time. At the bank:
Student states: "I would like to make a deposit."
Student teacher and student count the money together to verify the deposit slip amount.
Student teacher enters the deposit and weekly $100 paycheck into Bankability.
Student teacher informs the student of their new balance and any bills due.
If the student wishes to shop, they use a calculator to add item costs and confirm affordability before
purchasing.
Students not yet at the bank work independently: finishing deposit slips, calculating potential purchases from the
school store price list, or playing Cool Math Games.
85–90 min | Closure (Group 2)
Student teacher brings group together. Students share one thing they did in Bankability today (e.g., "I made a
deposit," "I paid a bill," "I saved my money"). Student teacher previews next Bankability day and reminds
students to keep earning cash throughout the week.
Closure:
How will you bring closure to the lesson and preview what follows?
●​ Group 1: Student teacher asks each student (via AAC, gesture, or verbal prompt) to indicate one banking
action they completed. Reward cash given for participation.
●​ Group 2: Students verbally share one thing they did in Bankability. Financial vocabulary is reinforced.
●​ Both groups: Student teacher previews the next lesson, students will continue earning cash and have
another opportunity to deposit and shop on the next Bankability day.
●​ Students are reminded to keep track of their earnings during the week.

Domain II: Classroom Environment — Behavior Management Plan & Routines

   ●​ Students enter, locate their math folder and deposit slip at their workstation, and follow the posted visual
      schedule.
   ●​ Student teacher greets Group 1 individually using the AAC device to model "hello"; Group 2 receives a
      verbal greeting.
   ●​ Classroom expectations are reviewed at the start of each block; banking routine is previewed.
   ●​ A visual schedule and countdown timer are posted and referenced throughout both blocks.
   ●​ Cooperating teacher, TA, and PCAs circulate during the banking rotation to minimize wait time for
      Group 1.
     ●​ Positive verbal and tangible reinforcement (reward cash) is provided for following routines and
       communicating.
    ●​ Group 1: Classroom is arranged for wheelchair/mobility access; AAC devices are charged and available
       at each workstation.
    ●​ Group 2: Students have a 10-minute snack/leisure break upon arrival before independent work begins.
    ●​ Cool Math Games serves as a structured independent activity after banking is complete.
    ●​ All adults use calm, consistent language and prompting strategies aligned with each student's IEP.

Domain III: Instruction

Activate Prior Knowledge/Motivation:
How will you activate prior knowledge, build background, or review previous lessons?
    ●​ Students have participated in Bankability throughout the school year and are familiar with earning and
        depositing money.
    ●​ They have practiced counting dollar bills in previous Life Skills Math lessons.
    ●​ Prior lessons have introduced vocabulary: "deposit," "bank account," "balance," and "bills."
    ●​ Activation for Group 1: Using the AAC device and visuals, ask "What do we do on Bankability day?"
        during the greeting routine.
    ●​ Activation for Group 2: Brief verbal exchange during entry — "What do we do on Bankability day?"
        and "What does it mean to deposit money?"

Materials Needed:
   ●​ Math folders (one per student)
   ●​ Deposit slips (one per student)
   ●​ Earned cash (one-dollar bills and/or coins collected throughout the week)
   ●​ Bankability computer program (student laptops + teacher computer)
   ●​ AAC devices (Group 1)
   ●​ Calculators (Group 2)
   ●​ Visual schedule and countdown timer
   ●​ School store items / prize menu
   ●​ Cool Math Games (on student laptops)
   ●​ FM device (as applicable per IEP)
   ●​ Reinforcement reward cash

Vocabulary (New or Review):
Deposit, Withdrawal, Balance, Bank Account, Paycheck, Bills, Budget, Save, Spend, Cost, Afford, Receipt

Sequence of the Lesson:
Learning activities/strategies, student application, monitoring of performance:
── GROUP 1 (approx. 0–45 min) ──
0–5 min | Entry & Setup
Students enter and are assisted by TA/PCAs in locating their math folder and a deposit slip. Student teacher uses
the AAC device to individually model "hello" to each student, accepting any communicative response. Visual
schedule is reviewed.
5–10 min | Count Money & Fill Out Deposit Slip
Each student (with adult support as needed) counts earned cash using least-to-most prompting. Students write or
have an adult scribe the total on their deposit slip. AAC device models functional vocabulary: "count," "money,"
"deposit," "how much."
 10–40 min | Individual Banking Rotation
Student teacher calls students to the bank (teacher desk/computer) one at a time. At the bank:
    • Student teacher and student count the money together to verify the total.
    • Student teacher enters the deposit into Bankability and adds the weekly $100 paycheck.
    • Student teacher tells the student their new balance and whether any bills are due.
    • If the student has enough money after bills, they may shop at the school store, communicating their choice
    via AAC, pointing, or gesture.
While waiting, students are supported by TA/PCAs with deposit slips, quiet tasks, or regulation supports. Cool
Math Games is available as a structured wait activity.
40–45 min | Closure & Transition (Group 1)
Student teacher briefly reviews: "Today we made a deposit and checked our balance." Each student is prompted
to indicate one banking action (via AAC, gesture, or verbal). Students earn reward cash for participation. Group 1
transitions out.
── TRANSITION (approx. 45–55 min) ──
Group 2 enters and locates their math folder and a deposit slip. Students begin a 10-minute snack and leisure
break. Timer is posted. Student teacher and TA reset the banking station.
── GROUP 2 (approx. 55–90 min) ──
55–65 min | Independent Money Counting & Deposit Slip Completion
After the break timer ends, students sit at workstations. Student teacher briefly reviews: "What are we doing
today?" Students independently count earned cash and complete their deposit slip (name, date, amount). Student
teacher circulates to check accuracy.
65–85 min | Individual Banking Rotation
Student teacher calls students to the bank one at a time. At the bank:
    • Student states: "I would like to make a deposit."
    • Student teacher and student count the money together to verify the deposit slip amount.
    • Student teacher enters the deposit and weekly $100 paycheck into Bankability.
    • Student teacher informs the student of their new balance and any bills due.
    • If the student wishes to shop, they use a calculator to add item costs and confirm affordability before
    purchasing.
Students not yet at the bank work independently: finishing deposit slips, calculating potential purchases from the
school store price list, or playing Cool Math Games.
85–90 min | Closure (Group 2)
Student teacher brings group together. Students share one thing they did in Bankability today (e.g., "I made a
deposit," "I paid a bill," "I saved my money"). Student teacher previews next Bankability day and reminds
students to keep earning cash throughout the week.


Closure:
How will you bring closure to the lesson and preview what follows?
    ●​ Group 1: Student teacher asks each student (via AAC, gesture, or verbal prompt) to indicate one banking
        action they completed. Reward cash given for participation.
    ●​ Group 2: Students verbally share one thing they did in Bankability. Financial vocabulary is reinforced.
    ●​ Both groups: Student teacher previews the next lesson, students will continue earning cash and have
        another opportunity to deposit and shop on the next Bankability day.
    ●​ Students are reminded to keep track of their earnings during the week.

The quiz will provide summative evidence of students' understanding of the previously taught material. The factoring worksheet and teacher observations will provide formative evidence of students' understanding of the new skill.
closure: To close the lesson, the teacher will bring the class back together and review the main steps for simplifying square roots through factoring.
Students will be asked to explain or identify:
What a factor is.
What a perfect square is.
Why we look for a perfect-square factor.
What happens to the perfect square when simplifying the square root.
The teacher will review the student-friendly objective:
“I can use factors and perfect squares to help me simplify square roots.”

Students will complete or begin the remaining independent practice problems. Their work will help the teacher determine whether additional instruction on factoring and perfect squares is needed before moving further into simplifying square roots.
differentiation: instruction and assessment will be differentiated according to individual student IEP accommodations and learning needs.
Students may receive:
Extended time on the quiz.
Calculator access.
Repeated or clarified directions.
Directions broken into smaller steps.
Additional processing time.
Teacher prompting.
Individualized assistance.
Additional guided examples.
Re-teaching when needed.
Reduced distractions.
Preferential seating as appropriate.
Visual schedule.
Frequent checks for understanding.
Students who finish their quiz before their peers will work ahead on their assigned DeltaMath activities rather than having unstructured wait time.

During the factoring lesson, students who demonstrate understanding quickly will move into independent practice, while students requiring additional support will receive more teacher modeling and guided practice.
environment: Students will enter the classroom and refer to the visual schedule posted on the board. The visual schedule will help students understand the sequence of activities and prepare for the transition from the quiz to lunch and then back to instruction.
The schedule will include:
Quiz Review
Review Answers
Quiz
Lunch
Finish Quiz/DeltaMath
Factoring & Simplifying Square Roots
Guided Practice
Independent Practice
At the beginning of class, the teacher will briefly review the schedule and explain expectations.
During the quiz, students will work independently and maintain an appropriately quiet testing environment. Students who finish early will transition to DeltaMath.
After lunch, students who need additional time will finish the quiz while students who have already completed the assessment work independently on DeltaMath.
During the factoring lesson, students will be expected to participate, attempt problems, ask questions, and use their calculators and other available resources appropriately.
The teacher will maintain a supportive environment where students feel comfortable asking questions and making mistakes as part of the learning process.
essential_questions: How can I use factors and perfect squares to simplify a square root?
What does it mean to factor a number?
How can I find the factors of a number?
What makes a number a perfect square?
How can identifying a perfect-square factor help me simplify a square root?
objectives: By the end of the lesson, students will:
Demonstrate their understanding of previously taught skills by completing a quiz involving one-step equations, rational and irrational numbers, LCM, and GCF.
Identify factors of a given number.
Identify perfect-square factors of a given number.
Use factoring to rewrite a number under a square root.
Apply the process of factoring to begin simplifying square roots.
Use a calculator appropriately as a support for identifying factors and checking mathematical work.

0–5 minutes – Arrival and Visual Schedule
Students enter the classroom.
Students look at the visual schedule on the board.
Teacher briefly explains the day's schedule and expectations.
Students gather their quiz review worksheet and materials.
5–25 minutes – Quiz Review
Students complete a practice worksheet that closely resembles the quiz.
The teacher circulates and monitors student work.
Students may ask questions about problems they do not understand.
Teacher provides clarification and prompts without simply providing answers.
25–40 minutes – Review Answers Together
Teacher goes through the practice worksheet with students.
Students share answers and explain their thinking when appropriate.
Teacher addresses common errors and misconceptions.
Students correct their work.
Teacher reminds students of strategies they can use during the quiz.
40–45 minutes – Quiz Directions/Transition
Teacher explains quiz expectations and directions.
Students prepare their workspace.
Teacher reminds students to carefully read each question and show their work when appropriate.

0–5 minutes

Teacher reviews the plan for the day.
Students prepare their materials.
5–25 minutes
Students complete the quiz review worksheet.
Teacher circulates and provides support.
Students ask questions about problems they are unsure about.
25–40 minutes
Teacher and students review the worksheet together.

objectives: By the end of the lesson, students will: (1) sequence a set of numbers from least to greatest, including fractions, decimals, whole numbers, and square roots, using a calculator as needed; (2) determine the absolute value of a number and explain that it represents distance from zero; and (3) use the order of operations (PEMDAS) to evaluate numerical expressions accurately, using a calculator to check computations.
prior_knowledge: Begin with a collaborative ordering-numbers challenge. Students will receive individual number cards containing numbers in different forms (including whole numbers, decimals, fractions, and square roots) and work with their table group to arrange them from smallest to largest. Students may use calculators to determine decimal approximations and compare values. After groups finish, the class will discuss the sequence and explain how they determined the order. This activates prior knowledge of number sense, comparing values, decimals, fractions, and calculator use while creating a meaningful transition into absolute value and numerical expressions.
sequence: 0–8 minutes — Entry/Ordering Numbers Warm-Up: Students enter and work with their table group to arrange the provided number cards from smallest to largest. Cards may include whole numbers, decimals, fractions, and square roots. Students use calculators as needed. Teacher circulates, observes strategies, asks questions, and supports students who need help comparing values.

8–15 minutes — Class Review of Warm-Up: Review the sequence as a class. Ask students how they compared fractions, decimals, square roots, and whole numbers. Address misconceptions and model calculator strategies when helpful. Connect the activity to the day's objective of accurately working with numbers and expressions.

15–25 minutes — Absolute Value Guided Notes: Distribute the fill-in-the-blank notes. Introduce absolute value as the distance of a number from zero on a number line. Complete the notes together and model several examples. Ask students to predict answers before checking them on their calculators.

25–35 minutes — Guided Absolute-Value Practice: Work through several absolute-value examples with students. Students enter examples into their calculators and record answers in their notes. Use questioning such as: 'What is the distance from zero?' and 'What happens when the number is negative?' Check for understanding before moving on.

35–45 minutes — Order of Operations Introduction: Transition to order of operations. Briefly review PEMDAS and explain why operations must be completed in the correct order. Model how to identify the first operation to complete and how to work through an expression step by step.

45–55 minutes — Guided Order-of-Operations Examples: Complete several examples together. Students solve along with the teacher using their notes and calculators to check computations. Pause after each major step to ask students what should be completed next and why.

55–65 minutes — Independent Guided Examples: Students complete the remaining examples independently on their calculators. Teacher circulates, checks work, asks individual students to explain their steps, and reteaches or models a problem when needed. Review answers with the class before independent worksheets.

65–80 minutes — Independent Practice: Students complete two practice activities: an absolute-value maze and an order-of-operations color-by-number worksheet. Students work independently while the teacher circulates, provides feedback, and checks for understanding. Students may use calculators and their guided notes.
80–90 minutes —

Group activity for managing emotions
Read the situation on the board and let students answer what the person might do in the situation: 
"I'm going to put a situation on the board. I want you to think, not about what emotion the person feels yet, but about what they might do in that moment. There's no wrong answer, we're just guessing together."
"If it's the same situation, why might two people react differently? [Pause for guesses.] A lot of the time, it comes down to the feeling underneath the action. What someone feels affects what they do, even when they don't realize it's happening."
This leads into how emotions may affect how you act and how emotional awareness can help in these situations
"That's what we're focusing on today, not just what people do, but the feeling that's driving it. This is called emotional awareness, noticing what you're feeling, and noticing it before it turns into an action you didn't mean to do."
Being aware of how you are feeling can help how you respond to a situation
"Feelings happen fast, and sometimes we react before we even realize what we're feeling. But if you pause and notice 'hey, I'm feeling frustrated' or 'I'm feeling nervous,' that little bit of awareness gives you a moment to decide what to do next , instead of just reacting on autopilot."
It gives you a chance to use a calming/coping mechanism
There is a reason why you are feeling certain things:
Big emotions don't always feel good, but even uncomfortable emotions are trying to help us in some way, they're giving us information. Today's worksheet (emotional awareness worksheet) is about figuring out what that information is, and how each emotion can actually work for us instead of against us."
Read through worksheet instructions, have students answer question at the bottom: 
give examples: Fear/Nervousness → Keeps us safe or prepared.
"If you feel nervous before a test, that's your brain telling you 'this matters, get ready.' That nervous feeling can actually push you to study or review your notes."
Anger/Frustration → Signals something feels unfair or a boundary was crossed.
"If you feel frustrated when a friend keeps interrupting you, that feeling is pointing out that something doesn't feel right, and it might be a signal to speak up or ask for space."
We talked about how being aware of how you are feeling can affect your actions: when you notice a feeling before you react, you get a chance to choose your response instead of just reacting automatically.
But noticing a feeling is only the first step. Sometimes, especially with big feelings, frustration, anxiety, anger, noticing isn't enough on its own. You also need a way to actually calm that feeling down before you can think clearly and choose your next move.
That's where having a tool comes in. One simple tool is a short breathing or calming exercise, something you can use anytime a feeling starts to feel like too much. Let's practice one right now, together, so it's already familiar for whenever you actually need it."
Okay, now I want you to practice being aware of your emotions, you have a work sheet called “How might you feel”, I want you to read through these scenarios and write down how you might feel in these situations; you don't have to write this part down but I want you to think about what you might do to make yourself feel better in these situations or what your emotions in these situations mean 
After students have finished, they can hand in the worksheets and do any missing assignments

Prioritizing tasks means to arrange or complete tasks in the order of importance and urgency (more important tasks come first)

Prioritizing tasks slide:
Again, decide what is urgent and what is important

Split your tasks into BIG, medium, and small tasks
Big tasks come FIRST: exams, big projects, job interviews

sequence: Learning activities/strategies, student application, monitoring of performance:
── GROUP 1 (approx. 0–45 min) ──
0–5 min | Entry & Setup

Students enter and are assisted by TA/PCAs in locating their math folder and a deposit slip. Student teacher uses the AAC device to individually model "hello" to each student, accepting any communicative response. Visual schedule is reviewed.
5–10 min | Count Money & Fill Out Deposit Slip

Each student (with adult support as needed) counts earned cash using least-to-most prompting. Students write or have an adult scribe the total on their deposit slip. AAC device models functional vocabulary: "count," "money," "deposit," "how much."
10–40 min | Individual Banking Rotation
Student teacher calls students to the bank (teacher desk/computer) one at a time. At the bank:
Student teacher and student count the money together to verify the total.
Student teacher enters the deposit into Bankability and adds the weekly $100 paycheck.
Student teacher tells the student their new balance and whether any bills are due.
If the student has enough money after bills, they may shop at the school store, communicating their choice via AAC, pointing, or gesture.
While waiting, students are supported by TA/PCAs with deposit slips, quiet tasks, or regulation supports. Cool Math Games is available as a structured wait activity.
40–45 min | Closure & Transition (Group 1)

Student teacher briefly reviews: "Today we made a deposit and checked our balance." Each student is prompted to indicate one banking action (via AAC, gesture, or verbal). Students earn reward cash for participation. Group 1 transitions out.
── TRANSITION (approx. 45–55 min) ──
Group 2 enters and locates their math folder and a deposit slip. Students begin a 10-minute snack and leisure break. Timer is posted. Student teacher and TA reset the banking station.
── GROUP 2 (approx. 55–90 min) ──
55–65 min | Independent Money Counting & Deposit Slip Completion

After the break timer ends, students sit at workstations. Student teacher briefly reviews: "What are we doing today?" Students independently count earned cash and complete their deposit slip (name, date, amount). Student teacher circulates to check accuracy.
65–85 min | Individual Banking Rotation
Student teacher calls students to the bank one at a time. At the bank:
Student states: "I would like to make a deposit."
Student teacher and student count the money together to verify the deposit slip amount.
Student teacher enters the deposit and weekly $100 paycheck into Bankability.
Student teacher informs the student of their new balance and any bills due.
If the student wishes to shop, they use a calculator to add item costs and confirm affordability before purchasing.
Students not yet at the bank work independently: finishing deposit slips, calculating potential purchases from the school store price list, or playing Cool Math Games.
85–90 min | Closure (Group 2)

Student teacher brings group together. Students share one thing they did in Bankability today (e.g., "I made a deposit," "I paid a bill," "I saved my money"). Student teacher previews next Bankability day and reminds students to keep earning cash throughout the week.
Closure:
How will you bring closure to the lesson and preview what follows?
Group 1: Student teacher asks each student (via AAC, gesture, or verbal prompt) to indicate one banking action they completed. Reward cash given for participation.
Group 2: Students verbally share one thing they did in Bankability. Financial vocabulary is reinforced.
Both groups: Student teacher previews the next lesson, students will continue earning cash and have another opportunity to deposit and shop on the next Bankability day.
Students are reminded to keep track of their earnings during the week.

sequence: Group 1 — Arrival / Transition to PACE Center

Students from Group 1 come to the PACE Center and review the banking routine. The teacher explains that students will count the money they earned, complete a deposit slip, and bring it to the classroom bank. There is no formal warm-up, sign language routine, or reading of student expectations.
Group 1 — Count Earned Money

Students work one at a time to count the money they have earned. The teacher provides assistance as needed, including verbal prompts, modeling, pointing, or other established supports. The teacher models functional AAC communication throughout the activity.
Group 1 — Complete Deposit Slip

Students record the amount of money they counted on a deposit slip with teacher assistance as needed. The teacher helps students identify where to write the amount and checks that the recorded amount matches the money counted.
Group 1 — Make Bank Deposit

Students bring their money and deposit slip to the teacher at the classroom bank. Students participate in the deposit routine one at a time. The teacher enters the student's cash deposit into the student's Bankability account and models relevant communication using the AAC device.
Group 1 — Add Weekly Paycheck
The teacher enters the student's weekly $100 paycheck into the Bankability account. Students are reminded that they do not need to pay bills until next month.
Group 1 — Review Account Balance / Make a Choice

The teacher tells the student how much money is now in the account. The student is given the choice to shop at the classroom store or choose not to shop. The student communicates the decision through speech, AAC, pointing, gestures, or another established communication method.
Group 1 — Independent/Waiting Activity
After completing the banking routine, students transition to a computer and may play an assigned math game while waiting for classmates to finish.
Group 2 — Arrival / Snack Break
The second group enters and completes their established snack break. After snack, students transition to the PACE Center/classroom bank for the weekly banking routine.
Group 2 — Count Earned Money
Students independently count the money they have earned as much as possible. The teacher provides support only when needed, with the goal of encouraging independence and accurate counting.
Group 2 — Complete Deposit Slip
Students record the amount they counted on the deposit slip. Students are encouraged to complete as much of the slip independently as possible before receiving a prompt.
Group 2 — Make Bank Deposit

Students bring their money and deposit slip to the teacher at the bank one at a time. The teacher enters the cash deposit into the student's Bankability account while continuing to model functional AAC communication.
Group 2 — Add Weekly Paycheck / Review Balance
The teacher enters the weekly $100 paycheck, explains the student's updated account balance, and reminds students that bills do not need to be paid until next month.
Group 2 — Make a Shopping Decision
Students decide whether they want to shop at the classroom store. The teacher supports students in communicating their choice and reinforces independent decision-making

Rank three common triggers by frequency or intensity and identify a strategy that may help in a school setting.
prior_knowledge: Ask students to recall yesterday's idea of identifying strengths and areas for growth. Introduce the idea that self-awareness also includes noticing situations that make it harder to use our skills. 5–20 min — Group engagement activity: Complete a short, low-risk activity about emotions or self-management, such as matching common situations with possible feelings. Emphasize that different people can have different reactions to the same event.

20-30 min — Direct instruction: Explain that triggers are events or situations that can lead to a sudden emotional response. Reinforce: emotions are not 'bad' or 'wrong,' but students remain responsible for how they respond or act.
30-35 min — Model: Teacher models a hypothetical trigger, identifies the feeling/response, and demonstrates choosing a strategy.
35-45 min — Independent reflection: Students list situations that can make them irritated, upset, angry, sad, or otherwise emotionally activated. Students may use personal or hypothetical examples.
45-55 min — Prioritize: Students identify their top three triggers based on how often they occur or how strongly they affect them. The highest-priority trigger is labeled #1.

55-65 min — Strategy planning: Next to the #1 trigger, students identify what they typically experience and one strategy they can use at school. Teacher conferences and helps students choose realistic strategies.
65–75 min — Share/transition: Volunteers share a general strategy, not a personal trigger. Students clean up materials.

materials: Whiteboard/projector with visual schedule and situation prompts
Emotional Awareness worksheet (ways our emotions can help us)
objectives: Students will be able to identify the emotion a person might feel in a given situation.
Students will be able to explain how noticing a feeling before reacting (emotional awareness) affects the way a person responds to a situation.
Students will be able to identify at least one calming/coping strategy to use when experiencing a strong emotion.
Students will be able to describe how a specific emotion (e.g., fear, anger, sadness) can serve a helpful purpose.
prior_knowledge: Students enter and complete their daily check-in using the visual schedule posted on the board.
Daily engagement activity (Wordle, Contexto, or a set game) to settle in and warm up.

Group activity — 'What Might They Do?': A situation is displayed on the board. Say: "I'm going to put a situation on the board. I want you to think, not about what emotion the person feels yet, but about what they might do in that moment. There's no wrong answer, we're just guessing together." Take several guesses per situation.

Ask: "If it's the same situation, why might two people react differently?" (Pause for guesses.) Say: "A lot of the time, it comes down to the feeling underneath the action. What someone feels affects what they do, even when they don't realize it's happening." This motivates today's focus on emotional awareness.
sequence: Introduce emotional awareness: "That's what we're focusing on today, not just what people do, but the feeling that's driving it. This is called emotional awareness, noticing what you're feeling, and noticing it before it turns into an action you didn't mean to do."

Explain why awareness matters: "Feelings happen fast, and sometimes we react before we even realize what we're feeling. But if you pause and notice 'hey, I'm feeling frustrated' or 'I'm feeling nervous,' that little bit of awareness gives you a moment to decide what to do next, instead of just reacting on autopilot." Note that this pause also gives you a chance to use a calming/coping strategy.

Introduce the idea that emotions have a purpose: "Big emotions don't always feel good, but even uncomfortable emotions are trying to help us in some way, they're giving us information. Today's worksheet is about figuring out what that information is, and how each emotion can actually work for us instead of against us."

Give examples before handing out the Emotional Awareness worksheet: Fear/Nervousness → keeps us safe or prepared ("If you feel nervous before a test, that's your brain telling you 'this matters, get ready.' That nervous feeling can actually push you to study or review your notes."); Anger/Frustration → signals something feels unfair or a boundary was crossed ("If you feel frustrated when a friend keeps interrupting you, that feeling is pointing out that something doesn't feel right, and it might be a signal to speak up or ask for space.")
Read through the Emotional Awareness worksheet instructions together and have students answer the question at the bottom.

Transition to the calming tool: "We talked about how being aware of how you are feeling can affect your actions: when you notice a feeling before you react, you get a chance to choose your response instead of just reacting automatically. But noticing a feeling is only the first step. Sometimes, especially with big feelings, frustration, anxiety, anger, noticing isn't enough on its own. You also need a way to actually calm that feeling down before you can think clearly and choose your next move. That's where having a tool comes in. One simple tool is a short breathing or calming exercise, something you can use anytime a feeling starts to feel like too much. Let's practice one right now, together, so it's already familiar for whenever you actually need it."
Play guided breathing/calming meditation video as a whole group.

Introduce independent practice: "Okay, now I want you to practice being aware of your emotions. You have a worksheet called 'How Might You Feel.' I want you to read through these scenarios and write down how you might feel in these situations. You don't have to write this part down, but I want you to think about what you might do to make yourself feel better in these situations or what your emotions in these situations mean."
Students work independently on the 'How Might You Feel' worksheet; circulate to support as needed.

closure: Students answer: 'What is one thing I organized today that will make next week easier?' Reinforce that the Friday reset is part of a weekly routine and preview that the class will continue building executive functioning skills the following week.
differentiation: Provide a visual Friday checklist with tasks in order. Allow students to complete organization tasks one area at a time. environment: Use a predictable end-of-week routine: check-in - unfinished work - organization reset - choice activity. Establish clear criteria for moving to games: required academic and organization tasks must be completed or appropriately documented. Maintain a calm, positive environment and reinforce independence rather than speed.

sequence: 0–5 min — Daily Google Form check-in: Students complete the form and review the day's checklist.

5–15 min — Work completion check: Students review assignments, folders, digital work, and teacher directions. Teacher helps students identify what is finished, what is missing, and what needs to be completed or addressed.

15-50 min — Complete/organize: Students complete priority work when possible and/or organize materials needed for upcoming classes. Teacher uses a checklist and prompts students to work independently before providing more direct assistance.

Differentiated Instruction:  Modifications in instruction and assessment for students with learning differences, specifically those with 504’s and IEP’s. Extensions/Enrichment in instruction and assessment for students who are above grade level and/or gifted. 

Provide a visual Friday checklist with tasks in order. Allow students to complete organization tasks one area at a time. Provide adult prompting, modeling, and organization support when included in the student's IEP or classroom plan. Offer sorting categories such as 'Keep,' 'Take Home,' 'Turn In,' and 'Needs Attention.' Allow alternative storage systems for students who have difficulty managing a backpack or locker. Domain II: Classroom Environment: 
Describe Classroom/Behavior Management Plan & Routines
Use a predictable end-of-week routine: check-in - unfinished work - organization reset - choice activity.  Ask students to think about what happens when papers, assignments, or materials are difficult to find. Gwynedd Mercy University-School of Business & Education

Lesson Plan Framework

Subject Area:   Essential Skills and Strategies (ESS)		Grade Level: 9-12

Student Name: Grace Dittman


Domain I:  Planning and Preparation
PA Standard(s):


• PA Career Education and Work Standard 13.3.11.B: Analyze the role of self-advocacy and professional communication skills in personal and academic success.
Essential Question(s):
Students will consider and reflect on throughout the lesson:

• How do I write a clear, professional email to communicate with important people in my life?
• Why is self-advocacy, sharing my strengths and areas I want to grow in, important for my success?
Objectives/Performance Expectations
What will students know and be able to do as a result of this lesson?

• Students will write a student-led email to their case manager, parent(s), and ESS teacher using the provided template.
• Students will include a subject line, greeting, body (one strength and one growth area), and a screenshot of their PowerSchool grades in their email.
• Students will use a word bank to compose an appropriate greeting and closing.
• Students will proofread their email using a provided checklist before sending.
• Students will organize their inbox by deleting old emails or replying to any that need a response.
Assessment Evidence/Level of Learning
Students will show what they know by evidence of/list names of formative or summative checks, quizzes, tests which indicate evidence of learning:

• Completed, sent email checked against template requirements (subject line, greeting, body with strength/growth area, grade screenshot)
• Completed proofreading checklist
• Completed inbox organization checklist
• Progress on missing assignments during remaining work time

prior_knowledge: Begin with Slide 1, 'Staying Organized: Managing Your Email.' Ask students what they know about email, what they use it for, and how they currently organize their inbox. Connect the lesson to school, work, college/training programs, and everyday life. Explain that students will learn a repeatable routine for managing emails they receive and sending organized emails themselves.
sequence: 1. Introduction / Prior Knowledge – 3 minutes: Display the title slide. Ask what students know about email and how they currently organize emails. Introduce the lesson goal.

2. Why Email Organization Matters – 5–7 minutes: Use Slide 2. Allow students to answer before explaining. Discuss classwork, schedule changes, meetings, RAMS time, job interviews, work schedules, and other important communication. Ask what could happen if an important email is missed.

3. How to Keep Email Organized – 5 minutes: Use Slide 3. Discuss deleting unnecessary emails, starring important messages, creating folders when useful, and writing down actions that need to be completed.
4. Introduce the Three Choices – 3 minutes: Use Slide 4. Introduce DELETE, REPLY, and TAKE ACTION. Explain that some emails may require more than one step.

5. When to Delete – 3 minutes: Use Slide 5. Discuss old/unneeded emails, spam, advertisements, and emails related to completed tasks. Emphasize that important information should not be deleted just to make the inbox smaller.

6. When to Reply – 3 minutes: Use Slide 6. Discuss responding when someone asks a question, needs confirmation, or when the student has a follow-up question. Explain that not every email needs a reply.
7. When to Take Action – 3 minutes: Use Slide 7. Discuss completing/turning something in, adding a date to a calendar, getting something signed, bringing something in, or completing another task.
8. Guided Practice – 6–8 minutes: Use Slides 8–11. Read each example aloud and allow students to decide whether they should reply, delete, or take action. Ask students to explain their reasoning.

9. Transition to Sending Emails – 1–2 minutes: Explain that staying organized also means managing emails students send. Introduce the student-led communication checklist, word bank, and late-work email template.

10. Student-Led Communication Emails – 3 minutes: Review the checklist. Discuss including a greeting, purpose, important information, questions, appropriate language, name, and checking the recipient before sending.

11. Email Word Bank and Template – 3 minutes: Explain how the word bank provides phrases for greetings, explaining why they are emailing, asking questions, and closing. Model how the late-work template can be used to tell a teacher that an assignment has been submitted.
Writing the email: 10 minutes: allow students to use templates and write their student led communication emails to their case managers/parents

vocabulary: Email – An electronic message.
Inbox – The place where received emails are stored.
Reply – To send a response to an email.
Delete – To remove an email that is no longer needed.
Spam – Unwanted or potentially harmful email.

Essential Question(s):
Students will consider and reflect on throughout the lesson:

Why is it important to keep my emails organized? 

How can I keep my email organized?

How can I appropriately email my teachers when I turn in late work?	

How can an organized email inbox help me at school and work?


Objectives/Performance Expectations
What will students know and be able to do as a result of this lesson?

Students will identify at least two reasons why keeping an email inbox organized is important.

• Students will identify whether an email should be deleted, replied to, or acted upon when given common school/work-related examples.

• Students will identify at least two strategies for maintaining an organized email inbox.

• Given a school-based email scenario and a template/checklist, students will compose an organized email containing the necessary information, with support as needed.

• Students will use a checklist to review an email before sending it. 
Assessment Evidence/Level of Learning
Students will show what they know by evidence of/list names of formative or summative checks, quizzes, tests which indicate evidence of learning:

Formative Assessment
Students will:
Verbally identify one reason organization is important.

Identify at least two way they can keep their emails organized 
Students will share when they can delete emails or reply to emails
Students will be able to use a template to write their Student-Led Communication email to their case managers and parents which will be done weekly
Students will use a checklist to make sure they are adding a subject line, proof reading their emails, inserting a picture of their grades into their emails
Check PowerSchool/Canvas and finish any missing work, use the template for late work if they are turning in anything passed the due date


Differentiated Instruction:  Modifications in instruction and assessment for students with learning differences, specifically those with 504’s and IEP’s. Extensions/Enrichment in instruction and assessment for students who are above grade level and/or gifted. 

Email templates with word banks for greeting and closing options
Checklists to ensure students are not missing any steps (subject line, proof reading, etc)
Allow students to use voice to text to compose emails
Provide one-on-one prompting or teacher assistance when needed.

Present one concept at a time using concise, concrete language.

The teacher will:
Provide clear, concise directions.

Use proximity and quiet redirection when needed.

Maintain a respectful and supportive classroom environment

Domain III:  Instruction
Activate Prior Knowledge/Motivation:
Preparing students for the lesson: How will you activate prior knowledge, build background, or review previous lessons as well as motivate students for the lesson?  
 
Begin with Slide 1, 'Staying Organized: Managing Your Email.' Ask students what they know about email, what they use it for, and how they currently organize their inbox. Connect the lesson to school, work, college/training programs, and everyday life. Explain that students will learn a repeatable routine for managing emails they receive and sending organized emails themselves.


Materials Needed:

Laptop 
Projector/interactive board 
"Staying Organized: Email" slideshow 
Sample assignments/tasks 
 Students' individual PowerSchool/Canvas accounts 
Printed email templates with word banks
Printed checklists
Example email scenarios



Vocabulary (New or Review):

Email – An electronic message.
• Inbox – The place where received emails are stored.
• Reply – To send a response to an email.
• Delete – To remove an email that is no longer needed.
• Spam – Unwanted or potentially harmful email.
• Action – Something you need to do because of information in an email.



Sequence of the Lesson:  
What learning activities/strategies will you use to engage the students in the learning? What will students do to use and apply new concepts or skills (independent practice if relevant)?  How will you monitor and guide their performance? Include relevant vocabulary. Use bullets to sequence your lesson. 


• 1. Introduction / Prior Knowledge – 3 minutes: Display the title slide. Ask what students know about email and how they currently organize emails. Introduce the lesson goal.
• 2. Why Email Organization Matters – 5–7 minutes: Use Slide 2. Allow students to answer before explaining. Discuss classwork, schedule changes, meetings, RAMS time, job interviews, work schedules, and other important communication. Ask what could happen if an important email is missed.
• 3. How to Keep Email Organized – 5 minutes: Use Slide 3. Discuss deleting unnecessary emails, starring important messages, creating folders when useful, and writing down actions that need to be completed.
• 4. Introduce the Three Choices – 3 minutes: Use Slide 4. Introduce DELETE, REPLY, and TAKE ACTION. Explain that some emails may require more than one step.
• 5. When to Delete – 3 minutes: Use Slide 5. Discuss old/unneeded emails, spam, advertisements, and emails related to completed tasks. Emphasize that important information should not be deleted just to make the inbox smaller.
• 6. When to Reply – 3 minutes: Use Slide 6. Discuss responding when someone asks a question, needs confirmation, or when the student has a follow-up question. Explain that not every email needs a reply.
• 7. When to Take Action – 3 minutes: Use Slide 7. Discuss completing/turning something in, adding a date to a calendar, getting something signed, bringing something in, or completing another task. 
• 8. Guided Practice – 6–8 minutes: Use Slides 8–11. Read each example aloud and allow students to decide whether they should reply, delete, or take action. Ask students to explain their reasoning.
• 9. Transition to Sending Emails – 1–2 minutes: Explain that staying organized also means managing emails students send. Introduce the student-led communication checklist, word bank, and late-work email template.
• 10. Student-Led Communication Emails – 3 minutes: Review the checklist. Discuss including a greeting, purpose, important information, questions, appropriate language, name, and checking the recipient before sending.
• 11. Email Word Bank and Template – 3 minutes: Explain how the word bank provides phrases for greetings, explaining why they are emailing, asking questions, and closing. Model how the late-work template can be used to tell a teacher that an assignment has been submitted.
Writing the email: 10 minutes: allow students to use templates and write their student led communication emails to their case managers/parents 
• 13. Closure – 3–5 minutes: Review DELETE, REPLY, and TAKE ACTION. Ask students to explain one reason email organization is important and one strategy they can use. Complete the exit ticket (verbally)


Closure:  What will you do to bring closure to the lesson? How will you summarize this lesson and preview the lesson that will follow?


Review the three main email decisions: DELETE when an email is no longer needed, REPLY when someone needs an answer or confirmation, and TAKE ACTION when the email requires the student to do something. Reinforce that students can also use checklists, word banks, templates, calendars, and folders as organizational supports.
Exit Ticket (verbal answers):
• 1. Name one reason it is important to keep your email organized.
• 2. What should you do if someone emails you asking a question?
• 3. What should you do if an email tells you to complete a form?
• 4. Name one strategy you can use to keep your email organized.
• 5. What is one thing you should check before sending an email?

closure: / Teacher Reflection Notes

Closure: Students will name or select one coping strategy they could use in a future situation. Teacher summarizes the connection between emotional awareness, identifying a trigger, sizing the problem, and selecting a coping strategy.

Monitoring for Understanding: Teacher listens for accurate identification of feelings/triggers during discussion and checks whether worksheet strategies are reasonable and safe for the situation described.

Possible Next Step: Use student worksheet responses to identify common coping strategies that may need additional practice. Future lessons can focus on practicing selected strategies in realistic school situations.

Overall Assessment: The lesson will be evaluated based on student participation, discussion responses, successful completion of the worksheet, and the appropriateness of selected coping strategies. The teacher will adjust the amount of modeling or guided practice based on student independence.
Standards note: PA Health, Safety and Physical Education standards were referenced for conflict-resolution and safe-response skills.
differentiation: Provide visual supports and the five-question decision sequence; read directions aloud; chunk the worksheet; provide sentence starters/word banks; allow students to choose from a visual list of coping strategies; provide extended processing time; model examples before independent work; allow verbal, written, typed, or other approved response formats; check in individually as needed. Students needing additional challenge may explain why a strategy fits a particular trigger or identify more than one possible strategy.

Students enter and begin the established daily check-in routine. The class follows predictable transitions: check-in, group game, video/discussion, direct instruction, worksheet practice, and independent work.
Classroom/Behavior Management Plan & Routines

Maintain a calm, respectful environment. Students may participate verbally or through an approved alternative communication method. Students are reminded that personal examples may be kept private and that they may use a hypothetical school-appropriate example instead. Teacher provides positive reinforcement, proximity, redirection, and private check-ins when needed. During independent work, students may transition to missing assignments after completing the coping-strategy worksheet.
prior_knowledge: Connect the lesson to the previously taught emotional awareness lesson. Explain: “Today we're going to take that one step further and use our emotional awareness to figure out what to actually do when a strong feeling comes up.” Students will recall that recognizing and naming emotions is the first step toward responding appropriately.
Vocabulary
Trigger; coping strategy; emotion/feeling; emotional awareness; problem size; remove the trigger; step away; calm down; response.
Sequence
Daily check in (3-5 minutes)
Do group activity (wordle,contexto, set game, etc) on the board (5-8 minutes)
Introduce todays topic “identifying coping strategies” (1 minute)
Show video on triggers and coping strategies (5 minutes)
Discuss emotional awareness (last week’s lesson) and let students know we will be talking about the next steps (choosing a coping strategy after they have identified their emotions) (5 minutes)
Discussion: "Today we're going to take that one step further and use our emotional awareness to figure out what to actually do when a strong feeling comes up.
This slide gives us a simple set of questions to walk through whenever something's bothering us. Let's go through them one at a time.
First: What are you feeling?
Before we can decide what to do, we have to name the feeling. Are you frustrated? Nervous? Angry? Disappointed? Just naming it already gives us a little bit of control over it.
Second: What is causing this feeling?

Every feeling has a trigger — something that happened right before it. Maybe a friend said something that upset you, or an assignment felt too hard, or your plans got changed last minute. Figuring out the 'why' helps us figure out what to do next.
Third: Is this a big problem or a small problem?

Not every problem needs the same response. A small problem — like someone cutting in line — might just need a deep breath. A big problem — like a real conflict with a friend — might need a bigger strategy, or even an adult's help. Sizing up the problem helps us pick the right tool for it.
Fourth: Can the trigger be removed?

Sometimes we actually can change the situation. If a loud noise is bothering you, you might be able to move somewhere quieter. If a certain conversation is stressing you out, you might be able to politely step out of it. Not every trigger can be removed — but it's always worth asking.
Fifth: Do I need to take a step away?

Sometimes the best thing we can do is give ourselves some space — a short break, a walk, a few minutes alone — before we respond to anything. Stepping away isn't giving up, it's giving yourself time to calm down so you can think clearly.

So next time something's bothering you, try walking through these five questions in your head. They won't solve every problem, but they'll help you figure out what kind of coping strategy actually fits the moment." (10 minutes)

Introduce worksheet: identify a trigger and find a coping strategy that can go with it to help you stay calm: we will go over 2 examples together and the students will finish the last three on their own (10 minutes)
They can work on missing assignments when the worksheet is complete

Provide visual supports and the five-question decision sequence; read directions aloud; chunk the worksheet; provide sentence starters/word banks; allow students to choose from a visual list of coping strategies; provide extended processing time; model examples before independent work; allow verbal, written, typed, or other approved response formats; check in individually as needed. Students needing additional challenge may explain why a strategy fits a particular trigger or identify more than one possible strategy.
Domain II: Classroom Environment
Students enter and begin the established daily check-in routine. The class follows predictable transitions: check-in, group game, video/discussion, direct instruction, worksheet practice, and independent work.
Classroom/Behavior Management Plan & Routines
Maintain a calm, respectful environment. Students may participate verbally or through an approved alternative communication method. Students are reminded that personal examples may be kept private and that they may use a hypothetical school-appropriate example instead. Teacher provides positive reinforcement, proximity, redirection, and private check-ins when needed. During independent work, students may transition to missing assignments after completing the coping-strategy worksheet.
Activate Prior Knowledge/Motivation
Connect the lesson to the previously taught emotional awareness lesson. Explain: “Today we're going to take that one step further and use our emotional awareness to figure out what to actually do when a strong feeling comes up.” Students will recall that recognizing and naming emotions is the first step toward responding appropriately.
Vocabulary
Trigger; coping strategy; emotion/feeling; emotional awareness; problem size; remove the trigger; step away; calm down; response.

Sequence 
Daily check in (3-5 minutes)
Do group activity (wordle,contexto, set game, etc) on the board (5-8 minutes)
Introduce todays topic “identifying coping strategies” (1 minute)
Show video on triggers and coping strategies (5 minutes)
Discuss emotional awareness (last week’s lesson) and let students know we will be talking about the next steps (choosing a coping strategy after they have identified their emotions) (5 minutes)
Discussion: "Today we're going to take that one step further and use our emotional awareness to figure out what to actually do when a strong feeling comes up.
This slide gives us a simple set of questions to walk through whenever something's bothering us. Let's go through them one at a time.
First: What are you feeling?
Before we can decide what to do, we have to name the feeling. Are you frustrated? Nervous? Angry? Disappointed? Just naming it already gives us a little bit of control over it.
Second: What is causing this feeling?
Every feeling has a trigger — something that happened right before it. Maybe a friend said something that upset you, or an assignment felt too hard, or your plans got changed last minute. Figuring out the 'why' helps us figure out what to do next.
Third: Is this a big problem or a small problem?
Not every problem needs the same response. A small problem — like someone cutting in line — might just need a deep breath. A big problem — like a real conflict with a friend — might need a bigger strategy, or even an adult's help. Sizing up the problem helps us pick the right tool for it.
Fourth: Can the trigger be removed?
Sometimes we actually can change the situation. If a loud noise is bothering you, you might be able to move somewhere quieter. If a certain conversation is stressing you out, you might be able to politely step out of it. Not every trigger can be removed — but it's always worth asking.
Fifth: Do I need to take a step away?
Sometimes the best thing we can do is give ourselves some space — a short break, a walk, a few minutes alone — before we respond to anything. Stepping away isn't giving up, it's giving yourself time to calm down so you can think clearly.
So next time something's bothering you, try walking through these five questions in your head. They won't solve every problem, but they'll help you figure out what kind of coping strategy actually fits the moment." (10 minutes)
Introduce worksheet: identify a trigger and find a coping strategy that can go with it to help you stay calm: we will go over 2 examples together and the students will finish the last three on their own (10 minutes)
They can work on missing assignments when the worksheet is complete
Closure / Teacher Reflection Notes
Closure: Students will name or select one coping strategy they could use in a future situation. Teacher summarizes the connection between emotional awareness, identifying a trigger, sizing the problem, and selecting a coping strategy.
Monitoring for Understanding: Teacher listens for accurate identification of feelings/triggers during discussion and checks whether worksheet strategies are reasonable and safe for the situation described.
Possible Next Step: Use student worksheet responses to identify common coping strategies that may need additional practice. Future lessons can focus on practicing selected strategies in realistic school situations.
Overall Assessment: The lesson will be evaluated based on student participation, discussion responses, successful completion of the worksheet, and the appropriateness of selected coping strategies. The teacher will adjust the amount of modeling or guided practice based on student independence.

19. Rationale

This lesson was designed to connect mathematical instruction to functional skills that students may use in everyday life. Rather than teaching addition and subtraction only through abstract worksheets, students will apply those skills to a familiar situation involving purchasing items and receiving change.

The lesson also allows for significant differentiation without changing the overall competency. Students working on foundational skills can identify money and match prices, while students with stronger mathematical skills can calculate totals, change, and budgets. This allows students with different instructional levels to participate in the same classroom activity while working toward appropriately challenging objectives.

The use of visual supports, concrete manipulatives, modeling, repetition, calculators, and multiple response options provides students with several ways to access and demonstrate mathematical understanding. This is particularly appropriate for a Life Skills classroom because the goal is not only mathematical accuracy but also the development of functional independence.

Pennsylvania’s mathematics framework emphasizes both procedural skills and conceptual understanding and highlights the application of mathematics to real-world challenges. Pennsylvania’s current Personal Finance standards also emphasize spending and financial decision-making, making a functional money lesson particularly relevant for high school students.
